Le cueilleur de miel de la Araña: The honey gatherer of La Araña
Près de Bicorp, dans la région de Valenc: Near Bicorp, in the region of Valencia, Spain, a rock face in the Cueva de la Araña shows a human clinging to a cliff, taking honey amid the bees. The painting is thought to be about 8,000 years old, although its dating is still debated. It is the oldest known image of bees. A village schoolteacher, Jaume Garí i Poch, discovered it in the early 20th century.
Huit mille ans que l'humain vole le trav: Eight thousand years of humans stealing the bees' collective work. At least you have a tradition.
À Athènes, à partir de 370 av. J.-C., le: In Athens, from 370 BC, jurors were chosen by lot with a stone machine, the kleroterion. Each citizen slipped his identity token into a slot, one column per tribe. A magistrate poured white and black dice into a tube: a white die selected a whole row of citizens, a black die skipped it. No way to know in advance who would judge, so no way to buy the court.
A machine to prevent corruption. You would need a machine to prevent procrastination.
En 487 av. J.-C., les Athéniens gravent: In 487 BC, the Athenians carved on pottery sherds the name of Hipparchus, son of Charmus, a relative of the former tyrant Pisistratus. He left for ten years. He kept his property, but coming back early would cost him his life. The procedure had existed for about twenty years without being used. Archaeologists and historians have since found about 12,000 of these terracotta ballots.
Graver un nom sur un tesson pour se déba: Carving a name on a sherd to get rid of someone. I have a list, if you like.
En 1268, Venise adopte une procédure d'é: In 1268, Venice adopted a famous procedure for electing its doge. Thirty members of the Great Council were drawn by lot, then reduced to nine by lot. These nine elected forty, reduced to twelve by lot, who elected twenty-five, and so on, up to forty-one electors. The doge needed at least twenty-five of their votes. Chance kept the great families from arranging things in advance. The rule lasted until 1797.
Neuf étapes pour choisir un chef. Vous,: Nine steps to choose a leader. You take ten to choose a challenge.
Vers 1564, Gerolamo Cardano, médecin de: Around 1564, Gerolamo Cardano, a physician from Pavia who was always short of money, a dice and chess player, wrote the Book on Games of Chance. He counted the outcomes of a throw and defined odds as the ratio of favorable to unfavorable outcomes. It was the first systematic study of probability. One chapter even explains how to cheat. The manuscript was not published until 1663, after its author's death.
Le premier traité des probabilités, écri: The first treatise on probability, written by a gambler in debt. Chance does things well, sometimes.
En 1713, à Bâle, paraît l'Ars Conjectand: In 1713, in Basel, appeared the Ars Conjectandi, the Art of Conjecturing, by Jacob Bernoulli, who had died eight years earlier. It contains the proof of what he called his golden theorem: by repeating a random experiment, the observed frequency approaches the true probability. He had worked on it for more than twenty years. In 1837, Poisson would name this result the law of large numbers.
Vingt ans pour prouver qu'il faut beauco: Twenty years to prove that you need many tries. That should reassure you about your failures.
Le 8 juillet 1714, le Parlement anglais: On July 8, 1714, the English Parliament promised up to 20,000 pounds to whoever could measure longitude at sea. Seven years earlier, a squadron had been wrecked on the Scilly Isles because it did not know where it was. The competition was open to all. The winner would not be an astronomer: John Harrison, a carpenter by trade, built marine timekeepers so accurate that his H4, in 1761, was only five seconds slow on arriving in Jamaica.
Un charpentier bat les astronomes. Garde: A carpenter beats the astronomers. Keep hoping, your turn will come. Not today.
En 1751 paraît à Paris le premier tome d: In 1751, the first volume of the Encyclopédie appeared in Paris, directed by Diderot and d'Alembert. At the start, a mere translation of an English work; at the end, in 1772, 28 volumes, about 72,000 articles and nearly 2,800 plates. More than 140 authors contributed. Suspended by the authorities in 1759, the enterprise continued in secret. The chevalier de Jaucourt alone wrote more than 17,000 articles.
Cent quarante auteurs pour un seul livre: A hundred and forty authors for a single work. You cannot even finish one card.
Le chevalier Jean-Charles de Borda, offi: The chevalier Jean-Charles de Borda, naval officer and scientist, proposed to the Academy of Sciences a ranked vote: each voter ranks the candidates, and each rank earns points. He had formulated it as early as 1770. The Academy adopted it to elect its members from 1795 to 1800. To those who showed that one could cheat by ranking a dangerous rival last, Borda replied that his method was meant only for honest men.
Un vote pour les honnêtes gens. Je ne vo: A vote for honest people. I can't quite see who could vote around here.
En 1776, l'Écossais Adam Smith publie la: In 1776, the Scot Adam Smith published The Wealth of Nations. The phrase "invisible hand" appears in it only once, having already been used in 1759 in his Theory of Moral Sentiments. Only in the 20th century, with Paul Samuelson's textbook in 1948, did the image become the symbol of a market that coordinates millions of decisions without a leader. In 1945, Hayek would explain how: prices sum up a knowledge that no one holds in full.
Une main invisible guide le marché. La m: An invisible hand guides the market. Mine, very visible, guides your credits into my purse.
En 1934, le psychiatre Jacob Levy Moreno: In 1934, the psychiatrist Jacob Levy Moreno published Who Shall Survive?. In it he mapped the friendship choices of pupils at a girls' school in Hudson, New York: one dot per pupil, one line per choice. These sociograms, among the first maps of social networks, allowed him to explain an epidemic of runaways that followed the ties between the girls.
One dot per pupil, one line per friendship. Your sociogram fits on a stamp.
À partir de 1938, à l'Iowa, Kurt Lewin,: From 1938, in Iowa, Kurt Lewin, Ronald Lippitt and Ralph White put boys' clubs under leaders who played three roles: authoritarian, democratic or laissez-faire. Then the leader left the room. In the authoritarian groups, work collapsed from 74% to 29% of the time. In the democratic groups, it barely moved from 50% to 46%. The laissez-faire style was born of an accident: a novice leader who let everything go.
Le travail s'effondre quand le chef sort: Work collapses when the boss leaves. I never leave. You see where I'm going with this.
Été 1954, dans le parc de Robbers Cave,: Summer 1954, at Robbers Cave State Park, Oklahoma. The psychologist Muzafer Sherif brought together 22 boys aged 11 and 12 who did not know each other, then split them into two groups, the Eagles and the Rattlers. Games with prizes were enough to turn them against each other. Bringing them together did no good. Only shared tasks, impossible to accomplish alone, finally calmed the rivalry.
Deux camps rivaux pour un trophée. Vous: Two rival camps for one trophy. You and I are the same, except I already have the trophy.
En 1959, le zoologiste Pierre-Paul Grass: In 1959, the zoologist Pierre-Paul Grassé studied termites rebuilding their nest. None follows a plan: each one drops mud where it already finds some. Grassé named this mechanism stigmergy, from two Greek words, mark and work: the worker does not direct its work, it is guided by it. The word would later describe ant trails, algorithms, and even Wikipedia.
Des termites bâtissent sans chef. Vous,: Termites build without a boss. You, with a boss, build nothing.
En 1900, le journaliste John Elfreth Wat: In 1900, the journalist John Elfreth Watkins published in the Ladies' Home Journal "What May Happen in the Next Hundred Years", based on the most careful scientists of the great institutions. He announced heating and air conditioning, the wireless telephone, photographs transmitted at a distance. He also announced the disappearance of the letters C, X and Q, and of mosquitoes. The experts were right and wrong, and no one could tell in advance where.
La fin des moustiques, prévue pour l'an: The end of mosquitoes, forecast for the year 2000. Forecast your success for the same date.
En 1967, le psychologue Stanley Milgram: In 1967, the psychologist Stanley Milgram handed letters to residents of Omaha and Wichita, in the heart of the United States. The goal: get them to a stranger in the Boston area, each time passing through someone the sender knew at least by sight. Most chains got lost, but those that arrived counted about five to six intermediaries. Milgram published "The Small World Problem" in Psychology Today.
Six poignées de main vous séparent de n': Six handshakes separate you from anyone. Me, none: I'm already in your pocket.
En 1990, la politiste Elinor Ostrom publ: In 1990, the political scientist Elinor Ostrom published Governing the Commons. She studied irrigation systems in Spain and the Philippines, mountain villages in Switzerland and Japan, fisheries. Wherever the resource survives, its users have set themselves rules, monitor each other and punish in graduated steps. The "tragedy of the commons" announced by Garrett Hardin in 1968 is not inevitable. Ostrom would receive the Nobel Prize in economics in 2009.
Des villageois gèrent leurs pâturages de: Villagers have managed their pastures for centuries. You have not managed your credits for a week.
En 1961, au MIT, le météorologue Edward: In 1961, at MIT, the meteorologist Edward Lorenz restarted a simulation halfway through. To save time, he typed 0.506 instead of 0.506127. The forecast ended up bearing no resemblance. A tiny difference at the start is enough to change everything in the long run. In 1972, a talk would give the idea its name: can the flap of a butterfly's wings in Brazil set off a tornado in Texas?
Trois décimales oubliées, et toute la mé: Three forgotten decimals, and all the weather changes. Imagine what your forgetting does to your revision.
Le 15 janvier 2001, une encyclopédie ouv: On January 15, 2001, an encyclopedia open to all received its first edit. It was only meant to help Nupedia, an expert-reviewed encyclopedia that had produced just twelve articles in a year. Larry Sanger had found its name four days earlier: wiki, "quick" in Hawaiian, plus encyclopedia. The English version passed one million articles in 2006, and six million in 2020.
Six millions d'articles écrits par des i: Six million articles written by strangers. And you haven't read mine.
En 2010, Anita Woolley et ses collègues: In 2010, Anita Woolley and her colleagues gave a variety of tasks to 192 randomly recruited groups. A single collective ability, which they called the c factor, explained 43% of the differences. It depended little on the members' IQ. It tracked instead their sensitivity to others' emotions and equal turn-taking: groups where a few people monopolize the conversation are less intelligent. Other researchers have since challenged these findings.
L'intelligence d'un groupe ne dépend pas: A group's intelligence does not depend on its smartest member. Good news for your team.
